PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
These taxes are based on the property’s value.
Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate.
One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year.
...
***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.
One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts.
Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.

## Proposition 42
**The basics**
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes.
But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound.
And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026.
It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
...
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
...
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other.
If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
...
The measure states that its purpose is to protect Californians’ ability to save for retirement and the future, though opponents say it’s meant to trick voters into canceling the billionaire tax.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

These taxes are based on the property’s value.

A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

**The basics**
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes.
But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound.
And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026.
It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

So this is California's November 3, 2026 General Election Proposition 42: "Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment."

Key facts so far:
- Prop 42 prohibits new state taxes on ownership of personal property (financial assets, retirement accounts, savings, etc.) and limits retroactive taxes.
- It would nullify conflicting taxes enacted after January 1, 2026.
- Critically, it interacts with Proposition 40 ("billionaire tax") — a one-time 5% tax on net worth of California billionaires. If Prop 42 gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 could be voided even if both pass.
- Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council, AMVETS. Funding in support: ~$128 million (likely billionaire-funded, per opponents).
- Opponents: Bernie Sanders, SEIU United Healthcare Workers West. Funding in opposition: ~$22.7 million.
- The "against" campaign contact email is info@YesOn40.com — suggesting the opposition to 42 is tied to the Yes on 40 campaign.

Let me research more:
1. The LAO analysis in full.
2. Arguments and rebuttals.
3. News coverage: LAist, LA Times, CalMatters, etc.
4. Who is funding Yes on 42 (e.g., billionaires like Sergey Brin, Larry Page?).
5. What Prop 40 is — the billionaire tax, one-time 5% wealth tax to fund healthcare (to offset federal Medicaid cuts?).

Let me fetch the LAO analysis and the arguments page, plus news coverage.

Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Ballot Label

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

‘Billionaire tax’ Prop 40 and its rival props 41 and 42
We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Under Proposition 42, the state would not be able to institute any new taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts, other than real estate. It would also prevent most new taxes from being applied retroactively.
Understanding Prop. 42
Proposition 42 is partly an effort to block another measure voters will see on their ballot, Proposition 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax). Also known as the billionaire’s tax, Proposition 40 seeks to establish a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires in California. (You can read more about Proposition 40 here (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax).)
Proposition 42 would effectively kill Proposition 40, even if both measures pass: If Proposition 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax could be declared void, according to an analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) from the California Secretary of State.
For example, under Proposition 40, a billionaire subject to the tax would have to pay based on their accumulated wealth, including wealth from their intellectual property and artwork and jewelry they have in the state. Proposition 42 would make it so such assets cannot be taxed.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) :
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Sponsored message
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A "no" vote means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Here's what supporters say
California's high cost of living and taxes have made living in the state difficult, and Proposition 42 aims to put a cap on any attempt to go further. For example: California’s constitution currently allows for taxes on things people own, such as art on display in a home, that haven't generated any taxable revenue. Proposition 42 would block such taxes.
Notable endorsements: Los Angeles and Orange Counties Building and Construction Trades Council; California Professional Firefighters; California Society of Certified Public Accountants; several business groups, including the Valley Industry and Commerce Association and Greater Los Angeles African American Chamber of Commerce.
Here's what opponents say
They criticize Proposition 42 for shielding billionaires from paying a one-time tax to help stabilize the healthcare system in California.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party; SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West; supporters of Proposition 40.
Potential financial impact
The California Secretary of State’s analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) found that, if approved, Proposition 42 could make it harder for the state to raise taxes in the future: “This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.”
What it takes to win
A majority is needed to pass.

‘Billionaire tax’ Prop 40 and its rival props 41 and 42
We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Under Proposition 42, the state would not be able to institute any new taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts, other than real estate. It would also prevent most new taxes from being applied retroactively.
Understanding Prop. 42
Proposition 42 is partly an effort to block another measure voters will see on their ballot, Proposition 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax). Also known as the billionaire’s tax, Proposition 40 seeks to establish a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires in California. (You can read more about Proposition 40 here (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax).)
Proposition 42 would effectively kill Proposition 40, even if both measures pass: If Proposition 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax could be declared void, according to an analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) from the California Secretary of State.
For example, under Proposition 40, a billionaire subject to the tax would have to pay based on their accumulated wealth, including wealth from their intellectual property and artwork and jewelry they have in the state. Proposition 42 would make it so such assets cannot be taxed.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) :
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Sponsored message
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A "no" vote means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Here's what supporters say
California's high cost of living and taxes have made living in the state difficult, and Proposition 42 aims to put a cap on any attempt to go further. For example: California’s constitution currently allows for taxes on things people own, such as art on display in a home, that haven't generated any taxable revenue. Proposition 42 would block such taxes.
Notable endorsements: Los Angeles and Orange Counties Building and Construction Trades Council; California Professional Firefighters; California Society of Certified Public Accountants; several business groups, including the Valley Industry and Commerce Association and Greater Los Angeles African American Chamber of Commerce.
Here's what opponents say
They criticize Proposition 42 for shielding billionaires from paying a one-time tax to help stabilize the healthcare system in California.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party; SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West; supporters of Proposition 40.
Potential financial impact
The California Secretary of State’s analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) found that, if approved, Proposition 42 could make it harder for the state to raise taxes in the future: “This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.”
What it takes to win
A majority is needed to pass.

‘Billionaire tax’ Prop 40 and its rival props 41 and 42
We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Under Proposition 42, the state would not be able to institute any new taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts, other than real estate. It would also prevent most new taxes from being applied retroactively.
Understanding Prop. 42
Proposition 42 is partly an effort to block another measure voters will see on their ballot, Proposition 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax). Also known as the billionaire’s tax, Proposition 40 seeks to establish a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires in California. (You can read more about Proposition 40 here (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax).)
Proposition 42 would effectively kill Proposition 40, even if both measures pass: If Proposition 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax could be declared void, according to an analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) from the California Secretary of State.
For example, under Proposition 40, a billionaire subject to the tax would have to pay based on their accumulated wealth, including wealth from their intellectual property and artwork and jewelry they have in the state. Proposition 42 would make it so such assets cannot be taxed.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) :
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Sponsored message
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A "no" vote means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Here's what supporters say
California's high cost of living and taxes have made living in the state difficult, and Proposition 42 aims to put a cap on any attempt to go further. For example: California’s constitution currently allows for taxes on things people own, such as art on display in a home, that haven't generated any taxable revenue. Proposition 42 would block such taxes.
Notable endorsements: Los Angeles and Orange Counties Building and Construction Trades Council; California Professional Firefighters; California Society of Certified Public Accountants; several business groups, including the Valley Industry and Commerce Association and Greater Los Angeles African American Chamber of Commerce.
Here's what opponents say
They criticize Proposition 42 for shielding billionaires from paying a one-time tax to help stabilize the healthcare system in California.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party; SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West; supporters of Proposition 40.
Potential financial impact
The California Secretary of State’s analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) found that, if approved, Proposition 42 could make it harder for the state to raise taxes in the future: “This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.”
What it takes to win
A majority is needed to pass.

‘Billionaire tax’ Prop 40 and its rival props 41 and 42
We dive deep into Prop 40 and its rival props, 41 and 42, and what's at stake.
Under Proposition 42, the state would not be able to institute any new taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts, other than real estate. It would also prevent most new taxes from being applied retroactively.
Understanding Prop. 42
Proposition 42 is partly an effort to block another measure voters will see on their ballot, Proposition 40 (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax). Also known as the billionaire’s tax, Proposition 40 seeks to establish a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires in California. (You can read more about Proposition 40 here (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/2026-election-california-general-prop-40-billionaire-tax).)
Proposition 42 would effectively kill Proposition 40, even if both measures pass: If Proposition 42 gets more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax could be declared void, according to an analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) from the California Secretary of State.
For example, under Proposition 40, a billionaire subject to the tax would have to pay based on their accumulated wealth, including wealth from their intellectual property and artwork and jewelry they have in the state. Proposition 42 would make it so such assets cannot be taxed.
Official title on the ballot: Prohibits new state personal property taxes and certain retroactive state taxes
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/index.htm) :
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Sponsored message
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A "no" vote means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Here's what supporters say
California's high cost of living and taxes have made living in the state difficult, and Proposition 42 aims to put a cap on any attempt to go further. For example: California’s constitution currently allows for taxes on things people own, such as art on display in a home, that haven't generated any taxable revenue. Proposition 42 would block such taxes.
Notable endorsements: Los Angeles and Orange Counties Building and Construction Trades Council; California Professional Firefighters; California Society of Certified Public Accountants; several business groups, including the Valley Industry and Commerce Association and Greater Los Angeles African American Chamber of Commerce.
Here's what opponents say
They criticize Proposition 42 for shielding billionaires from paying a one-time tax to help stabilize the healthcare system in California.
Notable opponents: California Democratic Party; SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West; supporters of Proposition 40.
Potential financial impact
The California Secretary of State’s analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/analysis.htm) found that, if approved, Proposition 42 could make it harder for the state to raise taxes in the future: “This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.”
What it takes to win
A majority is needed to pass.

## Proposition 40

### Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments.
Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
## Proposition 41
### Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it.
This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
## Proposition 42
### Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other.

- Opponents of 42: SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders, California Democratic Party.

- Newsom (a Democrat) opposes Prop 40 and endorsed Prop 42.
- Some traditional Democratic allies (Planned Parenthood, California Teachers Association) oppose Prop 40 because of budget concerns.
- Prop 42 protects ordinary Californians' 401(k)s, pensions, IRAs from future wealth taxes — not just billionaires. There have been multiple legislative proposals to tax wealth in recent years (ACA 8/AB 259 wealth tax proposals).
- Prop 40's polling is underwater (46% yes, 52% no per PPIC late October; prediction markets <30%), so it may fail anyway — but Prop 42 ensures it and sets a permanent constitutional protection.

Arguments for No on 42:
- It's a billionaire-funded "poison pill" designed to kill Prop 40 and permanently ban wealth taxes, funded overwhelmingly by billionaires ($128M vs $23M).
- Prop 40 would raise tens of billions for healthcare to offset federal Medicaid cuts that could leave 3.4M Californians without coverage; 90% goes to healthcare.

Honestly, I think the stronger public-interest case is "no" for these reasons:

1. Prop 42 is a permanent, sweeping constitutional prohibition enacted in response to one specific, temporary measure. Constitutional amendments that permanently foreclose entire categories of future policy are generally bad governance — they lock in the preferences of today's wealthiest donors against future democratic choice. California already suffers from ballot-box budgeting and constitutional straitjackets (Prop 13, Prop 98, Gann limit).

2. The "protect your retirement" framing is largely a pretext. Prop 40 explicitly excludes pensions and retirement accounts. Legislative wealth-tax proposals (e.g., AB 259/ACA 8) targeted households with $50M+ net worth, not ordinary savers. The measure's backers spent $128M not to protect ordinary retirees but to shield ~200 billionaires from a one-time 5% tax.

3. The retroactivity concern about Prop 40 could have been addressed without a permanent ban on all personal property taxation. Prop 42's breadth reveals its purpose: not fairness about retroactivity, but permanently immunizing wealth from taxation.

4. Meanwhile, the stakes against Prop 42 are concrete: California faces ~$30B/year in federal Medicaid cuts, with up to 3.4M people potentially losing coverage. Prop 40 offers tens of billions for healthcare. Prop 42's passage (with more votes) would kill that.

- Prop 40's retroactivity may make it unconstitutional, so the healthcare money may be illusory.
- Wealth taxes have failed in Europe; most countries repealed them due to capital flight and administrative costs.
- California's dependence on ~200 people for a big chunk of revenue makes driving them away genuinely dangerous.
- Bipartisan-ish opposition to Prop 40 (Newsom, business, some labor) suggests it's flawed.

Still, a voter could vote no on 40 AND no on 42 — defeating the billionaire tax directly without permanently amending the constitution. Voting no on 42 preserves the legislature's and voters' future options; it doesn't enact any tax. Voting yes on 42 permanently amends the constitution at the behest of billionaires.

Actually, that's the cleanest way to see it: A no vote on 42 doesn't impose any tax; it merely preserves the status quo option. A yes vote permanently removes a policy tool forever, as a poison pill funded by the wealthiest people in the state to defeat a specific healthcare funding measure. The measure's popular framing (protect retirement) doesn't match its actual content (permanently banning wealth taxation of any kind, including prospective taxes on billionaires).

Also, note the measure nullifies taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 — it's written to kill Prop 40 retroactively even if Prop 40 passes. That's precisely the kind of special-interest constitutional tinkering that's bad practice.

I'm fairly convinced the better answer is "no."

Now I have a comprehensive picture, including editorial positions:

**Editorials against Prop 42 (No):**
- Press Democrat: No — "takes an entire class of taxes off the table for good"
- SF Chronicle: No — "poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40"; "California isn't coming for your retirement"
- Daily Californian: No
- Mercury News/East Bay Times: No on all of 40, 41, 42 — "Reject billionaires tax — and billionaires' attempts to shackle state's fiscal future"

**Editorials for Prop 42 (Yes):**
- San Bernardino Sun / OC Register / San Diego Union-Tribune (SCNG editorial board): Yes — limits taxation, retroactive taxes are unreasonable
- Gov. Newsom endorsed Yes on 42

**Key analytical points:**
- Prop 42 is one of two billionaire-funded "poison pills" (41 and 42) designed to kill Prop 40.
- Funded ~$128M by billionaires (Brin, Schmidt et al.) vs ~$23M opposition.
- There are NO active proposals to tax retirement accounts (CalMatters: "There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature."). The "protect your retirement" framing is misleading — Prop 40 explicitly excludes pensions/retirement accounts, and past legislative wealth tax proposals targeted $50M+ households.
- Prop 42 is broader than needed: it permanently amends the constitution to ban an entire class of taxes, forever, including prospective, well-designed wealth taxes. Mercury News: "shackle state's fiscal future."
- Prop 42 also bans retroactive taxation generally, which could hamper the state's ability to prevent tax avoidance (e.g., closing loopholes retroactively, preventing people from dodging known upcoming taxes) — per CalBudget's Kayla Kitson.
- The retroactivity ban is the "reasonable-sounding" part, but Prop 40's retroactivity concern can be addressed by voting no on 40 itself.

Now, deciding: The question asks me to determine whether it's "better" to vote yes or no.

The case for "no" is quite strong from a good-governance and democratic standpoint:
1. A no vote imposes nothing; it preserves options. A yes vote permanently amends the state constitution to eliminate an entire category of taxation — a drastic, permanent response to one temporary measure.
2. If a voter dislikes Prop 40, they can simply vote no on Prop 40. Prop 40 was already trailing in the polls (46% yes/52% no in late October PPIC poll; prediction markets <30%). The poison pill is unnecessary for that purpose.
3. Prop 42's marketing ("protect retirement") is deceptive — no proposals exist to tax retirement accounts, and Prop 40 excludes them. It's funded overwhelmingly by billionaires ($128M vs $23M) who personally stand to save billions.
4. Retroactive tax bans sound good but also remove the state's anti-avoidance tools.
5. Constitutional ballot-box budgeting is a known pathology in California; adding another straitjacket is bad policy.
6. The measure was explicitly designed to subvert the democratic outcome on Prop 40 — even if a majority of voters approve Prop 40, Prop 42 could nullify it.

The case for "yes":
1. Wealth taxes are economically risky; billionaire flight is real (Page, Brin, Thiel, Kalanick left). California's reliance on top earners makes it vulnerable. LAO: possible ongoing income tax revenue loss < $1B/year.
2. Retroactive taxation is unfair — Prop 40 taxes people based on residency on Jan 1, 2026, before the vote. Constitutional concerns could void it in court anyway, leaving a legal mess.
3. Newsom (Democratic governor) endorsed it; conservative editorial boards back it; public safety unions back it.
4. Protection against future legislative wealth taxes that might expand thresholds downward over time.

Weighing: The retroactivity provision of Prop 42 is the only genuinely meritorious part, and it's bundled with a permanent, sweeping prohibition designed by billionaires to protect billionaires. The Mercury News editorial captures the balanced view: reject both the wealth tax AND the billionaire-backed shackles. But between yes and no on Prop 42 itself, a no vote is safer and more democratic: it doesn't enact any tax, preserves future flexibility, and resists a deceptive, self-dealing campaign. A voter worried about the billionaire tax can vote no on 40 directly.

Also, polling suggests Prop 42 could pass with more votes than 40 and nullify a democratically-approved wealth tax — a subversion of majority rule that editorial boards across the spectrum flagged.

My answer: no.

Let me also quickly double check the "six proposals to tax retirement" claim — the Yes on 42 side claims the Legislature introduced six proposals to tax retirement/savings. CalMatters says past legislative proposals (e.g., AB 259/ACA 8 by Lee) targeted net worth over $50M — not retirement accounts of ordinary people. The claim that they would "tax retirement and savings accounts" of ordinary Californians is exaggerated. CalMatters explicitly says: "There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature." That confirms the deceptive framing.

I've done extensive research. Final answer: no.

- San Bernardino Sun / OC Register / San Diego Union-Tribune (SCNG editorial board): Yes — limits taxation, retroactive taxes are unreasonable
- Gov. Newsom endorsed Yes on 42

**Key analytical points:**
- Prop 42 is one of two billionaire-funded "poison pills" (41 and 42) designed to kill Prop 40.
- Funded ~$128M by billionaires (Brin, Schmidt et al.) vs ~$23M opposition.
- There are NO active proposals to tax retirement accounts (CalMatters: "There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature."). The "protect your retirement" framing is misleading — Prop 40 explicitly excludes pensions/retirement accounts, and past legislative wealth tax proposals targeted $50M+ households.
- Prop 42 is broader than needed: it permanently amends the constitution to ban an entire class of taxes, forever, including prospective, well-designed wealth taxes. Mercury News: "shackle state's fiscal future."
- Prop 42 also bans retroactive taxation generally, which could hamper the state's ability to prevent tax avoidance (e.g., closing loopholes retroactively, preventing people from dodging known upcoming taxes) — per CalBudget's Kayla Kitson.
- The retroactivity ban is the "reasonable-sounding" part, but Prop 40's retroactivity concern can be addressed by voting no on 40 itself.

Now, deciding: The question asks me to determine whether it's "better" to vote yes or no.

The case for "no" is quite strong from a good-governance and democratic standpoint:
1. A no vote imposes nothing; it preserves options. A yes vote permanently amends the state constitution to eliminate an entire category of taxation — a drastic, permanent response to one temporary measure.
2. If a voter dislikes Prop 40, they can simply vote no on Prop 40. Prop 40 was already trailing in the polls (46% yes/52% no in late October PPIC poll; prediction markets <30%). The poison pill is unnecessary for that purpose.
3. Prop 42's marketing ("protect retirement") is deceptive — no proposals exist to tax retirement accounts, and Prop 40 excludes them. It's funded overwhelmingly by billionaires ($128M vs $23M) who personally stand to save billions.
4. Retroactive tax bans sound good but also remove the state's anti-avoidance tools.
5. Constitutional ballot-box budgeting is a known pathology in California; adding another straitjacket is bad policy.
6. The measure was explicitly designed to subvert the democratic outcome on Prop 40 — even if a majority of voters approve Prop 40, Prop 42 could nullify it.

The case for "yes":
1. Wealth taxes are economically risky; billionaire flight is real (Page, Brin, Thiel, Kalanick left). California's reliance on top earners makes it vulnerable. LAO: possible ongoing income tax revenue loss < $1B/year.
2. Retroactive taxation is unfair — Prop 40 taxes people based on residency on Jan 1, 2026, before the vote. Constitutional concerns could void it in court anyway, leaving a legal mess.
3. Newsom (Democratic governor) endorsed it; conservative editorial boards back it; public safety unions back it.
4. Protection against future legislative wealth taxes that might expand thresholds downward over time.

Weighing: The retroactivity provision of Prop 42 is the only genuinely meritorious part, and it's bundled with a permanent, sweeping prohibition designed by billionaires to protect billionaires. The Mercury News editorial captures the balanced view: reject both the wealth tax AND the billionaire-backed shackles. But between yes and no on Prop 42 itself, a no vote is safer and more democratic: it doesn't enact any tax, preserves future flexibility, and resists a deceptive, self-dealing campaign. A voter worried about the billionaire tax can vote no on 40 directly.

Also, polling suggests Prop 42 could pass with more votes than 40 and nullify a democratically-approved wealth tax — a subversion of majority rule that editorial boards across the spectrum flagged.

My answer: no.

Let me also quickly double check the "six proposals to tax retirement" claim — the Yes on 42 side claims the Legislature introduced six proposals to tax retirement/savings. CalMatters says past legislative proposals (e.g., AB 259/ACA 8 by Lee) targeted net worth over $50M — not retirement accounts of ordinary people. The claim that they would "tax retirement and savings accounts" of ordinary Californians is exaggerated. CalMatters explicitly says: "There are no active proposals to tax those accounts on the ballot or in the Legislature." That confirms the deceptive framing.

I've done extensive research. Final answer: no.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.

Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property's value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
Proposal
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more "yes" votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters. This is because the courts could find that Proposition 42 conflicts with Proposition 40.
Fiscal Effect
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future.
